> Before any model: what are you predicting, from what, and how will you know
> if it worked?

## Learning objectives

1. Split data into training and test sets, and explain why the split comes first.
2. Define overfitting and demonstrate it.
3. Fit a baseline model and use it as the bar to clear.
4. Choose an evaluation metric appropriate to the class balance.

## The setup

Supervised learning has three pieces: **features** (what you know), a **target**
(what you want to predict), and a **loss** (how wrong you were).

Everything else is detail.

## The discipline that matters

::: {.callout-important}
## Split before you look
Hold out a test set at the very beginning, before plotting, before choosing
features. Every decision you make while looking at data is a way for the test
set to leak into the model.
:::

```{r}
#| eval: false
set.seed(42)
n <- nrow(data)
train_idx <- sample(seq_len(n), size = 0.7 * n)
train <- data[train_idx, ]
test  <- data[-train_idx, ]   # do not touch until the end
```

With small biological datasets, a single split is noisy. Cross-validation reuses
the data more efficiently — but the principle is unchanged: the evaluation data
must never inform the model.

## Demonstrating overfitting

Fit models of increasing flexibility and watch training error fall while test
error rises. The gap between the two curves *is* overfitting. Seeing it once is
worth more than reading about it ten times.

## Always fit a baseline

Before anything sophisticated, fit the dumbest reasonable model:

- Classification → predict the majority class.
- Regression → predict the mean.

This is your bar. A model that cannot beat it has taught you something valuable
and cheap.

## Picking a metric

| Metric | Good for | Fails when |
|---|---|---|
| Accuracy | Balanced classes | Classes are imbalanced |
| Sensitivity | Catching cases | Cost of false alarms is high |
| Specificity | Ruling out | Missing cases is costly |
| AUC | Overall ranking | You need a single decision threshold |

::: {.callout-warning}
## The imbalance trap
At 95% negative, predicting "negative" always scores 95% accuracy. Report
sensitivity and specificity, and always state the base rate.
:::

## Exercises

1. Split a dataset 70/30 and fit a majority-class baseline. What accuracy do you
   get, and what does it tell you about the class balance?
2. Fit progressively more flexible models and plot training vs test error.
   Where do the curves diverge?
3. Construct a case where a 95%-accurate model is useless.

## Takeaways

- Split first. Everything else is downstream.
- The baseline is the bar.
- Choose the metric before you see the results.
